data.title: The security logic of the crypto industry has been completely rewritten.
data.description:
Author: Gu Yu, ChainCatcher

If the crypto industry's biggest fear in the past few years was a bug in a blockchain smart contract, then now, project teams should probably be more worried about: an employee attending a seemingly normal online interview or partner meeting and downloading insecure software.

On October 29th, Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, suffered an unprecedented security incident. Attackers, through multi-stage penetration, ultimately gained control of the exchange's internal wallet signature system, resulting in the impact of approximately $6.34 billion in digital assets.

This attack was not a traditional smart contract vulnerability exploit. According to Binance's preliminary investigation report released on November 3rd, the attackers had previously gained access to the core system step by step through fake job interviews, malware, compromised employee devices, and internal AI tools.

More importantly, this was not an isolated incident.

In September, Bitget suffered a security incident costing approximately $387.5 million, with attackers bypassing authorization controls to transfer assets by infiltrating the backend system of critical wallet infrastructure. In October, hardware wallets distributed through some of Ledger's Southeast Asian distribution channels were implanted with malicious components, resulting in the theft of user assets. In the first half of this year, projects such as Kelp DAO and Drift Protocol also suffered attacks worth hundreds of millions of dollars. From smart contracts to centralized exchanges, from employee computers to the hardware wallet supply chain, the crypto industry seems to be facing a security siege covering the entire industry chain. I. The most damaging vulnerabilities are no longer in the code. In the first decade or so of the crypto industry's existence, discussions about "security" mostly revolved around "whether there are vulnerabilities in on-chain smart contracts," which is fundamental to blockchain technology. However, today, most attacks and damage originate from outside of smart contracts. In CertiK's first-half report, the largest category of losses was wallet intrusion: 33 incidents, totaling $444 million, averaging over $13 million per incident. Phishing ranked second, with 63 incidents and $366 million. Although code vulnerabilities occurred 204 times, they only accounted for 11.5% of the losses. "What concerns me most is not the total amount, but the shape of the losses," said Ronghui Gu, co-founder and CEO of CertiK, in an interview with Forbes. He explained that nearly half of the losses in the first half of the year were concentrated in two incidents: Kelp DAO and Drift Protocol, totaling approximately $577 million. "Both of these stemmed from operational and infrastructure errors, not traditional code vulnerabilities." His explanation was straightforward: "Compared to finding vulnerabilities in the code, attacking key management, multi-signature governance, and operational infrastructure yields far greater returns." This path was repeatedly demonstrated this month. Ledger's problem wasn't with the chip, but with the reseller—the device was implanted before it even reached the user; Ngrave's problem wasn't with the wallet, but with the push notification provider being hijacked, followed by phishing; Polymarket's problem wasn't with its own system, but with a script from a UK website performance monitoring provider; Bloom Trading's problem was a remote code execution vulnerability in a third-party module; and on October 31st, at least 12 to 15 DeFi websites had their domains replaced with fake sites in the same batch of DNS hijackings. Governance is no exception. X100 suffered a $4.85 million loss due to a governance takeover by a flash loan in collusion with a Tornado Cash-funded address; Hifi Finance lost approximately $1 million after a malicious proposal was submitted by an address funded by Tornado Cash; Yapeswap's governance attack was even simpler—the quorum was set to zero. Data reveals the shifting direction of attack patterns: Ari Redbord, Global Policy Director at TRM Labs, points out that attacks targeting infrastructure and keys account for only 15% of all incidents, yet cause 76% of the losses. But what's more troublesome than "where the money went" is what happens after it's gone. For most projects, once attacked, the trust of users and the market is irreparably lost, even for established and well-known projects. Last November, Balancer lost $128 million in less than half an hour due to a rounding error in its v2 composable stable pool, affecting six chains. This August, this once-established protocol, which managed $7 billion, announced a phased shutdown. In an open letter, the team admitted that almost a year after the vulnerability, they still underestimated its impact on subsequent adoption rates: every subsequent collaboration had to start by explaining the vulnerability, resulting in longer decision-making cycles and smaller collaborations. The cost of a vulnerability is never just the theft itself. The question then arises: since the cost is so clear, why weren't the defenses strengthened accordingly? II. Technology is Advancing, But Attacks are Moving Faster. This dire situation forces us to consider: with technological advancements, the crypto industry should be becoming increasingly secure, so why is it becoming less secure? AI is one of the most noteworthy factors. In the past year, AI development has been phenomenal, with various models emerging. While countless crypto companies are integrating AI into their daily workflows, hackers are becoming increasingly adept at utilizing it. Microsoft, in its assessment on October 29th, stated that of the eight North Korean hacking groups it tracked, three had already integrated AI into their daily operations, and four others were rapidly expanding its use. They were using generative models to mass-produce fake job postings, customize interview scripts, and even directly assist in vulnerability discovery. SlowMist founder Yu Xian cited a case: Moonwell suffered a $1.78 million theft, with the problematic code marked "Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 4.6"—generated by AI and directly merged into the production environment. Security researcher Stacy Muur bluntly stated, "Encryption security is completely dead," and "We are entering a very serious cybersecurity arms race." Bankless co-founder Ryan Sean Adams warned that AI is giving hackers "dark superpowers," and "We don't have much time left." CZ also stated, "The AI ​​industry has not yet achieved a point where defensive capabilities precede offensive capabilities," and the industry can only "use AI to fight AI." An even more advanced risk is Agents. Gu Ronghui's assessment is: "An AI Agent with wallet access is essentially a new type of high-privilege key holder. The difference is that its decision-making process can be manipulated by external inputs, and while these abnormal humans might be able to detect them, an Agent without sufficient security constraints might not be able to identify them." CertiK documented a prototype: In June, the well-known arbitrage bot JaredFromSubway was lured by a fake arbitrage pool deployed by attackers, automatically approving malicious contracts and losing approximately $7.5 million. However, attributing everything to AI misses another half of the answer. The structural inadequacy of industry security investment is also a core factor. Crypto projects generally prioritize marketing over security, and audit reports often quickly become invalid after on-chain upgrades. The lazy screening logic of "looking at audits, checking TVL, and comparing APY" has completely collapsed. Dragonfly partner Haseeb Qureshi offers another perspective: DeFi thefts in 2026 amounted to approximately $1.89 billion annualized, lower than in 2025. While the number of attacks increased, the size of each attack decreased even faster—attackers are increasingly targeting smaller protocols and abandoned projects, as larger protocols have undergone more robust hardening. This precisely illustrates that the threat hasn't diminished, but rather that defensive resources are highly unevenly distributed: leading institutions have the capital to build defenses, while long-tail projects are left vulnerable. This uneven distribution of defensive resources is only one aspect; the other side involves adversaries who don't operate according to the cost structure of startups—North Korean hackers operating like state apparatuses. According to Chainalysis, North Korean-linked hackers stole approximately $2.02 billion in 2025, accumulating to approximately $6.75 billion over the years. This is not a disorganized, scattered effort, but an action system with a national budget, patience, and monthly planning—the UN expert group report explicitly links crypto theft to funding for North Korea's ballistic missile and nuclear weapons development. When the attacker is a state actor and the defender is a startup, the nature of this war has changed. Furthermore, new standards are creating new attack surfaces. In the Binance case, the attackers exploited the EIP-7702 account abstraction authorization mechanism, allowing hot wallets to delegate execution logic to malicious contracts—every step forward in innovation expands the attack surface. Defenses need to be strengthened in more and more places, and the windows that can be filled are often only opened after an incident. III. The Industry Re-discusses "Security" Binance's preliminary investigation report on November 3rd exposed its own shortcomings, detailing the specific methods hackers used to launch social engineering attacks. The report also revealed that since 2026, Binance's security team has detected and blocked 57 suspected North Korean-related cyber threats, ranging from fake job postings and malware disguised as popular development tools to tampered software packages and fake video conferencing applications. Industry discussions quickly shifted from "who did it?" to another question: once an employee is scammed and a computer is compromised, what defenses can prevent further losses? The same question applies to other cases this month—Ledger's resellers, Polymarket's third-party scripts, and the DNS hijacking on October 31st—none of which had their entry points within their own systems. CoinEx founder Yang Haipo attributed it to three avoidable mistakes: insufficient isolation between development and operations environments, lack of a second layer of verification in production operations, and failure to independently verify signing participants. His most pointed statement was that if all parties simply trust upstream requests, "even with a multi-signature architecture, it might behave no differently than a single signature"—these measures don't require complex technology, but rather a lack of discipline. AltLayer founder YQ shares a similar assessment: these attacks exceed the scope of smart contract auditing; defenders must understand the complete workflow between employee terminals, internal tools, and production clusters. However, simplifying incidents to "a few basic mistakes" is equally dangerous. SlowMist founder Yu Xian warns that only after an attack does one see how intelligence gathering, malicious code evasion, trust chain exploitation, lateral movement, and risk control bypassing are combined—this is an APT process; "seemingly crude methods, in the right target and work scenario, can still cause serious consequences." BitsLab co-founder Luis is even more direct: locking the screen cannot stop malicious software already implanted in the device; the cost of attack and defense is already vastly different, and AI will continue to amplify this asymmetry. Both sides agree on the conclusion: security is no longer something that a pre-deployment audit report can deliver. Gu Ronghui said that the industry is no longer facing "how to prevent individual vulnerabilities from being exploited," but rather a protection system covering the entire lifecycle of assets. Even if a link is compromised, the loss must be controlled locally. Yu Jianing pointed out that the management model based primarily on pre-deployment audits is no longer suitable, and continuous assessment, real-time monitoring, and emergency response need to be incorporated into routine governance. Going a step further, there is the only piece of good news in this round of incidents. On October 31, the FBI attributed the attack to North Korea's TraderTraitor operation. The Joint Secret Service and the IRS Criminal Investigation Department released hundreds of addresses involved in the case and called on THORChain node operators, instant exchange platforms, DeFi protocols, and blockchain analytics companies to intercept related transactions; Tether, Circle, and other issuers collectively froze approximately $3 billion. When one exchange was compromised, the entire industry's clearing and issuance processes were mobilized within a few dozen hours. However, collaboration changes the distribution of losses after they occur, not the probability of those losses. CertiK statistics show that in the first half of the year, the entire industry had $115 million in funds frozen or returned, accounting for 8.8% of the $1.316 billion in losses. Binance's recovery rate was surprisingly high because the stolen funds were mainly stablecoins, while Bitcoin and Ethereum, which lack issuers, were still held by attackers, amounting to approximately $2.4 billion. Conclusion From smart contract vulnerabilities to compromised employee devices, from third-party service provider intrusions to AI-assisted penetration, from governance attacks to the long-term plans of North Korean hacker groups, the crypto industry is undergoing a profound shift in attack patterns. AI further reduces the cost of attack preparation, professional attack groups continuously increase the scale and persistence of attacks, and the long-standing lack of security investment by project teams creates more opportunities for these attacks. Withdrawals from a project might be promptly suspended, an abnormal transaction might be frozen by the stablecoin issuer, and an attack might only result in user data breaches and compromised internal system privileges. But all these events signify that almost all crypto projects have lost control of their security boundaries. Blockchain can guarantee the immutability of transaction records, but it cannot guarantee that the person initiating the transaction hasn't been scammed, nor can it guarantee that the keys used to sign the transaction haven't been stolen. When attackers begin to bypass code and directly target individuals and organizations, the crypto industry needs to rethink what true security really is. If the most important innovation in the crypto industry over the past decade was establishing a value transfer system that doesn't require trusting third parties, then in the next decade, the industry must answer another question: How can we truly protect users' assets and trust in an environment filled with untrusted participants?

data.title: Does the peak in AI capital spending mean the peak in the US economy as well?
data.description:
Author: Zhao Ying, Wall Street Insights

AI capital expenditure is approaching a historical turning point, and the fate of US economic growth may be deeply intertwined with it.

According to TrendFocus, Jefferies strategist Christopher Wood warned in his latest report that financial markets have sent clear signals that the AI ​​capital expenditure cycle may have peaked through widening credit spreads and a continued decline in semiconductor stocks—the macro implications of this judgment extend far beyond the technology sector itself.

According to the Jefferies report, in the four quarters ending in the third quarter of 2026, US AI-related real capital expenditure will contribute as much as 1.39 percentage points to the year-on-year growth of real GDP, accounting for 67% of the overall growth rate of 2.1%. At the same time, investment in information processing equipment and software as a percentage of nominal GDP has risen to 5.35%, surpassing the 4.46% peak during the dot-com bubble in 2000, setting a new historical high.

This means that once AI capital expenditures contract substantially, the US economy will face a direct and significant downward shock. The market has already reacted. Semiconductor stocks continue to be under pressure, and the credit market has shown clear cracks: the spreads on 10-year corporate bonds for Amazon, Alphabet, and Meta have widened by 16, 16, and 35 basis points respectively from recent lows; while the spreads on 5-year CDS for Oracle and CoreWeave have surged to 329 and 1163 basis points respectively from early June lows. Meanwhile, with the Democrats regaining control of Congress after the US midterm elections, the market is concerned that their regulatory stance on data centers and AI models will further suppress AI spending expectations. The credit market is sounding the alarm, with consensus forecasts for AI spending facing downward revision pressure. The volatility in the credit market is the most direct market basis for the current theory that AI capital expenditure has peaked. A Jefferies report points out that the best way to assess the risks of AI capital expenditure is to continuously track AI-related credit spreads—and the current spread trend has given a clear signal of tightening. Specifically, data shows that the 10-year corporate bond yield spreads for Amazon, Alphabet, and Meta have risen from recent lows of 73, 65, and 94 basis points on October 12 to 89, 81, and 129 basis points, respectively. The 5-year CDS spreads for Oracle and CoreWeave surged from lows of 153 and 452 basis points in early June to highs of 329 and 1163 basis points respectively in late October. SoftBank's 5-year CDS spread also rose from a low of 278 basis points at the end of June to 442 basis points. The core implication of this signal is that the market is showing a growing willingness to finance AI-related investments. A Jefferies report suggests that this means there is a substantial risk of downward revision to the market consensus forecast for the combined capital expenditures of the four major hyperscale cloud service providers (Microsoft, Amazon, Alphabet, and Meta) in 2026—approximately $1.04 trillion. Hyperscale cloud providers are facing a cash flow crisis, and AI is eroding traditional businesses. The latest quarterly earnings reports have further exacerbated market concerns about the sustainability of AI capital expenditures. The four major hyperscale cloud service providers saw their combined capital expenditures increase by 108% year-on-year to $202 billion in the third quarter. However, at the same time, Amazon and Alphabet's free cash flow turned negative, reaching -$35 billion and -$9 billion, respectively. What's even more alarming for the market is that AI is beginning to erode the traditional core businesses of hyperscale cloud providers. Alphabet's Google search revenue growth slowed significantly from 19% year-on-year in the first quarter of 2026 to 12% in the third quarter, and search revenue's share of Alphabet's total revenue fell below 50% for the first time, dropping to 49.7%. Meanwhile, Google Cloud revenue surged 103% year-on-year to $30.7 billion, with its share rising from 20.7% to 24.1%. Amazon's online store revenue growth plummeted from 15% year-over-year in Q2 to 2% in Q3, while AWS revenue grew 39% year-over-year to $46 billion. The Jefferies report argues that the core motivation for hyperscale cloud providers' massive investment in AI is precisely their fear of AI disrupting their traditional businesses—a defensive rather than offensive spending logic that traps them in a prisoner's dilemma: "not spending money is waiting to die, spending money doesn't guarantee survival." The report specifically highlights a growing structural risk in the US AI ecosystem: the revolving financing system built around AI capital expenditures. The remaining performance obligations (RPO), i.e., the backlog of contract revenue, of the four major hyperscale cloud service providers (Microsoft, Amazon, Alphabet, and Oracle) rose to $2.5 trillion at the end of last quarter. Meanwhile, data center financing is increasingly taking off-balance-sheet forms, with hyperscale cloud providers partnering with private credit firms to establish "special purpose" investment vehicles. CoreWeave completed a $3.1 billion Deferred Drawing Rights (DDTL 5.0) financing in May of this year, the first known GPU-collateralized financing instrument issued through a public syndicated loan subsidiary, with its yield to maturity rising from 7.62% to 8.36%. It is estimated that the annual new issuance of data center asset securitization will reach $27 billion in 2025 and is projected to rise to $40 billion in 2026. A Jefferies report bluntly states that this system is extremely financially risky, unless it is assumed that parts of the US AI ecosystem are already considered "too big to fail." Microsoft's layoffs and cost reduction in China's AI sector foreshadow a paradigm shift in the industry. The potential inflection point in the AI ​​capital expenditure cycle has already left its mark on corporate behavior. Microsoft announced voluntary severance packages for approximately 60,000 eligible employees, representing more than a quarter of its global workforce. A Jefferies report suggests that the direct motivation for this move is cost-cutting under pressure from continuously escalating capital expenditure bills—despite Microsoft's positive free cash flow of $18.6 billion in the third quarter. Meanwhile, Desh Peramunetilleke, Global Head of Quantitative Strategy at Jefferies, pointed out in a mid-October report that the consensus earnings growth rate for global AI stocks is expected to slow significantly from approximately 100% in 2026 to 30% in 2027 and 22% in 2028, recommending that investors begin diversifying their portfolios beyond AI. In China, the logic of cost reduction has been present since the beginning of the AI ​​boom. Edison Lee, Head of Technology and Telecom Research at Jefferies China, points out that Chinese AI labs have consistently focused on computing efficiency. This stems from both the scarcity of computing power and the fact that Chinese AI has been driven by commercial application from the outset, rather than pursuing the Silicon Valley-style ultimate goal of AGI (Automatic Gaining Intelligence). This pragmatic approach may become the direction that the US AI industry is forced to emulate under the pressure of tightening financing. If AI spending comes to a screeching halt, US Treasuries will struggle to serve as a "safe haven." The Jefferies report clearly warns of the macroeconomic consequences of a sharp contraction in AI capital expenditure: this will have a direct negative impact on US economic growth and trigger a rapid reversal in the Federal Reserve's policy expectations from tightening to easing. However, the report also points out that in this scenario, US Treasury bonds will be unable to play the traditional role of a "safe haven asset." The reason lies in the "fiscal-driven" effect—the current US fiscal deficit has reached 6.2% of GDP, and historical patterns show that economic recessions typically expand the fiscal deficit by about 6 percentage points. Once the economy declines, the market will quickly shift its focus to the prospect of a sharp deterioration in fiscal revenue. At that point, the US Treasury market will behave more like a troubled emerging market than a traditional safe-haven asset. The report also cites Amara's Law, reminding investors that the short-term impact of new technologies is often overestimated, while the long-term impact is underestimated. Current market trends suggest that the global frenzy surrounding AI may have peaked. For investors, given the increasing uncertainty surrounding the AI ​​capital expenditure cycle, assets with lower correlation to AI capital expenditure, such as gold and biotechnology, may deserve more attention.

data.title: Why is the lucrative data center market facing resistance?
data.description:
Source: Blockworks; Author: Byron Gilliam; Translation: BitpushNews

In the eyes of the IRS, airports are giant ATMs.

Airports first incur property taxes, income taxes, and payroll taxes. But that's just the entry fee.

At Pittsburgh International Airport, parking incurs an additional 11.5% tax (on top of the regular sales tax). At Chicago O'Hare Airport, "franchise restoration fees" and "customer facilities fees" can increase car rental costs by up to 50%.

At each airport, passengers pay a 7.5% federal sales tax on their ticket price, a $5.30 "segmentation" fee per takeoff and landing, a $4.50 "passenger facilities fee" per departure airport, and an $11.20 TSA fee per round trip.

In total, a $150 ticket might incur an additional $60 in fees and taxes. These numbers accumulate quickly. By 2025, Dallas-Fort Worth International Airport will have paid approximately $14 billion in federal taxes, $5 billion in state taxes, and $3.4 billion in local taxes. (The airport also levies a 5% "venue tax" on car rentals, which funds the Dallas Mavericks' basketball arena.) But what about the planes arriving in and departing from Dallas? They likely pay nothing. Specialized leasing companies own about half of the world's commercial aircraft fleet, and most of these companies are legally registered in Ireland, where the corporate income tax rate is 15%. After deducting depreciation, the effective tax rate on the income from these aircraft is approximately zero. This is certainly a very profitable deal, and the reason these aircraft can be negotiated on such terms is because they are easily movable. Airports are treated so poorly in taxes because they are immovable assets. Dallas-Fort Worth International Airport can only be located in Dallas-Fort Worth. This is the "Ramsey Rule" of optimal taxation. Immovable assets such as airports, power plants, oil fields, hotels, and parking garages are taxed the heaviest because they have no bargaining power. No matter how much we tax them, they can't move. Movable assets such as airplanes, cargo ships, intellectual property, and wealth are taxed the lightest because they can shop around and find a better deal. Therefore, tax officials are usually eager to attract large immovable assets, such as data centers. However, taxpayers are not so enthusiastic. The Nasdaq plummeted this week because midterm election results suggest that data centers may no longer be welcome in the United States. There are 47 voting measures across the country that give voters the opportunity to restrict or ban data centers in their communities. Forty-six of these were approved. This is unwelcome news for a tax system that has so far failed to benefit from it. In Richland Parish, Louisiana, tax revenue from the Meta data center provided a $50,000 bonus for public school teachers. In Hoffman Estate, Illinois, tax revenue from the Microsoft data center will help build a new fire station. In Effinham County, Georgia, tax revenue from the OpenAI data center will fund a 40% reduction in local property taxes. In Loudoun County, Virginia, property taxes have declined year after year over the past decade thanks to revenue generated by numerous data centers. Loudoun County officials estimate that for every $1 of service consumed by data centers, $26 is taxed. Judging from the market's reaction to the midterm elections, you might think no one would want to take this deal anymore. But that may not be the case. Data centers remain popular, at least in Harwood, North Dakota—the only place where voters rejected measures restricting construction. They seem pleased with the data center under construction. “The sales tax and property tax are simply incredible for a small town like ours,” Mayor Blake Hankey said this morning, adding that the data center is expected to create more than 200 permanent jobs. Harwood has a population of 820. Data centers also remain popular in Alabama, where incoming Governor Tommy Tuberville is eager to make a deal. “We’re going to build data centers,” Tuberville said earlier this year. “The tax revenue from these things is incredible for schools, law enforcement, everything.” The governor-elect has also stated that he will place data centers in the state’s highest tax bracket. Like local utilities, data centers will be taxed at 30% of their property value. Imagine paying 30% of your home's value in taxes every year! If you were as immovable as a data center, you might have to do the same. Let's look at some charts. The people have spoken: In Nottingham, New Hampshire, the data center licensing moratorium passed with 90.3% of the vote. In Spring, Ohio, zoning restrictions barely passed with 52.6% of the vote. However, the single vote in favor of data centers was decisive: Harwood, North Dakota, rejected the restrictions by a 3-1 vote. Midterm Election Survey: The issue of data centers extends beyond specific measures. Nationwide, approximately 56% of voters rated data centers as a key or important factor in their vote for members of Congress. However, this is not the primary concern. Artificial intelligence and data centers rank far lower than the cost of living, the Iran war, ICE, and corruption. So why? Voters indicated that their primary concern regarding data centers was their "impact on resources," including water and electricity usage. Fortunately, modern data centers consume roughly the same amount of water as a local restaurant, and in some cases, they even reduce electricity bills for consumers.

Highest Tax Tier:

The Tax Foundation estimates that a data center in Santa Clara, California, will pay approximately $22 million in taxes on $33 million in revenue. That's an effective tax rate of 67%! (I'd welcome such a data center to my backyard :).

...

More than just property tax:

When a profitable object is immovable, taxes accumulate. In addition to property tax, corporate income tax, and sales tax, data centers also pay gross income tax (levied on revenue, not profit, oh dear) and tangible personal property tax (taxing the value of all items within the data center, such as servers, GPUs, and backup generators).

Made in the USA: The US has the majority of the world's data center capacity. But that may not last long. If data centers become unpopular in the US, they will seriously consider places like Malaysia. Or outer space! The midterm elections made Elon Musk's plans to build data centers in space seem less far-fetched. Has the job market never come to an end? Artificial intelligence doesn't seem to have caused many people to lose their jobs. Following the release of the data this morning, economist Jason Furman stated, "This is likely the best—or one of the best—job market we've ever seen." The tech apocalypse is here: Thursday's 4.4% sell-off in the S&P 500 was one of the worst 0.5% drops on record. This might be the right reaction: the stock market has already leveraged the massive investments hyperscale companies make in data centers, which will now be even harder to build. But I believe there will always be someone willing to take their money. If not, we have outer space. I wonder what the highest tax rate is on the moon?

data.title: BTC breaks $76,000; Solana's on-chain RWA value reaches $5 billion in October.
data.description:
Headline

▌BTC Breaks $76,000

Market data shows that BTC has broken through $76,000, currently trading at $76,004. The 24-hour decline has narrowed to 0.71%. Market volatility is high; please manage your risk accordingly.

▌Solana's On-Chain RWA Value Reaches $5 Billion in October

On November 6th, according to the Solana project team, its on-chain real-world assets (RWA) reached $5 billion in value in October, setting a new historical high; decentralized exchange trading volume reached $60 billion, the number of addresses holding stablecoins reached 14 million, and the cumulative spending on stablecoin cards reached $1 billion.

▌Former Chairman of the U.S. House Financial Services Committee: The Crypto Industry Missed Its Best Opportunity to Push for the Clarity Act and Bears Some Responsibility

On November 7, according to crypto journalist Eleanor Terrett, former U.S. House Financial Services Committee Chairman Patrick McHenry stated that the cryptocurrency industry botched the best opportunity to pass market structure legislation and admitted that he also bears some responsibility. In a candid conversation, he analyzed where the Clarity Act went wrong, the shortcomings of both the industry and legislators, and how the crypto industry should prepare in advance for a Democratic takeover of Congress in January.

Blockchain and AI Applications

▌OpenAI's New Funding Round: First Tranche of $11 Billion Received

On November 7th, according to sources, OpenAI's ongoing new funding round has received the first tranche of approximately $11 billion. This round values ​​the company at $1.25 trillion, and the total funding could reach up to $20 billion. The remaining funds are expected to arrive in the coming weeks. OpenAI previously planned to raise at least $30 billion at a valuation of $1.4 trillion, but subsequently reduced its funding target. In March of this year, the company completed a $122 billion funding round at a valuation of $852 billion.

Blockchain and AI Applications

▌OpenAI's New Funding Round: First Tranche of $11 Billion Received

Aave Labs Acquires Avon Team and Technology to Advance Fixed-Rate Lending On November 7th, Aave Labs acquired the team and technology of the on-chain lending protocol Avon to advance its fixed-rate lending business on its on-chain lending network. The transaction amount was not disclosed. The acquisition includes Avon's fixed and floating-rate lending protocols, on-chain order book, domain name, and related assets. Avon founders Prince Sinha and Ayush Kaul will join the Aave Labs engineering team, and Omar el-Ashaal will join its business development team. Aave Labs CEO Stani Kulechov stated that the Avon team will help Aave serve global institutions, fintech companies, and ordinary users, initially focusing on fixed-rate lending. Aave currently has over $30 billion in deposits and over $12 billion in active loans. Sources say Anthropic will launch its IPO roadshow next week. On November 7th, sources revealed that Anthropic plans to launch its formal initial public offering (IPO) roadshow next week, marketing to potential investors. This IPO roadshow comes after two weeks of sharp fluctuations in tech stocks. Previously, investors reacted to the massive AI spending plans announced by Amazon and Google, as well as the overwhelming victory of the Democrats in the midterm elections. While tech stocks rebounded last Friday, they still closed down 3% for the week. Anthropic is continuing to move forward with its listing plans, aiming to list the week of November 16th, before the US Thanksgiving holiday. The market had previously expected the company to raise more than $80 billion at a $1.5 trillion valuation, but recent market concerns about AI-related stocks and spending may prompt it to seek a lower valuation.

▌Uniswap Confirms Support for V4 Hooks on Hyperliquid L2 Project Elysium

On November 7th, according to HL HUB (Community), Uniswap confirmed support for V4 Hooks on the Hyperliquid L2 project Elysium. Developers can use Uniswap V4 Hooks to build customizable liquidity pools with features such as dynamic fees and custom trading logic. The Elysium mainnet is expected to officially launch on November 9th.

Google Invests $548 Million in Qualcomm Stake

▌Google Invests $548 Million in Qualcomm Stake

On November 7, according to a securities filing submitted on Friday, Google has purchased nearly 3 million shares of chipmaker Qualcomm, representing less than 0.5% of Qualcomm's total share capital. This investment will give Google business exposure as Qualcomm aggressively expands into the AI ​​data center market. The filing shows that the search giant spent approximately $548 million to purchase 2,976,982 shares of Qualcomm. In addition, Google also holds a stake in chip design company Arm and has entered into a stock agreement with chip design company Marvell for up to $12.2 billion, with the two companies collaborating on the development of Google's self-developed AI chip—the Tensor Processing Unit (TPU).

▌Circle mints 250 million new USDC on the Solana network

On November 7th, Whale Alert posted on the X platform that at 06:06 Beijing time today, the USDC Treasury minted 250 million new USDC on the Solana network, worth approximately $250 million. Solscan data shows that this transaction was executed by the Circle minting address.

▌Fidelity transfers 27,000 ETH to Galaxy Digital today

On November 7th, Onchain Lens posted on the X platform that Fidelity just transferred another 10,000 ETH to Galaxy Digital, worth approximately $22.32 million.

Since today, Fidelity has transferred a total of 27,000 ETH, worth approximately $60.27 million, to Galaxy Digital, possibly for sale. Arkham data shows that the transfers originated from the Fidelity Custody address.

Important Economic Developments

data.title: Anthropic Shareholder Report: China Model – The Most Valuable Enterprise Market
data.description:
Article by Sleepy

On November 3rd, Menlo Ventures, a veteran Silicon Valley venture capital firm, released its annual "State of Enterprise AI Report."

To understand how much money companies have spent this year, Menlo commissioned Morning Consult to survey AI decision-makers at nearly 400 US companies in September. These individuals handled over $4 billion in AI spending. According to Menlo's calculations, as of September this year, US companies had spent $176.8 billion on AI deployments, 5.4 times the $33 billion spent a year ago.

In September 2026, Chinese models accounted for 89% of open-source model spending by US companies. Kimi led the pack with a 61% share. (Image source: Menlo Ventures) This report, written for Silicon Valley, includes a set of figures: Chinese models account for nearly 90% of the production spending by US companies on open-source models. Kimi alone holds a 61% stake, followed by DeepSeek at 15%, GLM at 11%, and Qwen at 3%. Meta Llama, the leading Western open-source model, only has a 7% stake. Menlo Ventures, which wrote the report, is a major shareholder of Anthropic, leading its $750 million Series D round in 2024. In addition, Fireworks AI, the leading inference cloud that hosts Kimi on servers and sold to US companies, and whose annualized revenue just surpassed $1 billion this year, is a Menlo investment; OpenRouter, a model routing platform that processes 160 trillion tokens weekly, is a Menlo investment; and Cursor, specifically mentioned in the report, which trained Composer 2 on Kimi K2.5, is also a Menlo investment. If you only look at the report data, you might think that closed-source giants and the open-source camp should have been fighting to the death long ago, and that the models on both sides of the Pacific should be clearly divided. But adults consider pros and cons, while children divide into camps. Beyond these data and vested interests, Beating wants to understand why Kimi, in particular, has become the option that American companies are most willing to spend money on outside of closed-source flagships. To understand Kimi's "61%", we need to understand the strange spending habits of American companies on AI this year: the cheaper the model, the less people use it. For the past two years, the most popular prediction in the industry was that inference costs would decrease by 90% annually, and companies would eventually shift their workflows to cheaper, smaller models. Labs did indeed sell smaller models cheaper and cheaper. The result was exactly the opposite. From Q3 2025 to Q3 2026, the token share of small closed-source models like Haiku and Luna in the enterprise market dropped from 29% to 13%, a decline of more than half. Meanwhile, the most expensive flagship token saw its token share rise from 18% to 42%, and its spending share increase from 35% to 63%.

The share of cutting-edge models in enterprise AI spending and token usage is rising in tandem

Source: Menlo Ventures

A year ago, the most commonly used mainstays by US companies were Claude Sonnet 4.5 with an input of $3 and an output of $15 (per million tokens, the same below), and GPT-5 with $1.25 and $10 respectively. By this fall, however, everyone is lining up to switch to more expensive flagship models.

Frontier models are rising in share in enterprise AI spending and token usage in tandem

Source: Menlo Ventures

A year ago, the most commonly used mainstays by US companies were Claude Sonnet 4.5 with an input of $3 and an output of $15 (per million tokens, the same below), and GPT-5 with an input of $1.25 and $10 respectively.

Why are shrewd American companies suddenly abandoning their focus on cheap deals? The reason is simple: the work done by models has shifted from humans to agents. In February of this year, agent-driven traffic on OpenRouter officially surpassed human traffic; by the end of September, 80% of the tokens on the platform were generated by agents in the background, a 37-fold increase in just over six months. Of the $77.3 billion spent on enterprise AI applications, 76% was concentrated on programming and enterprise agents. The logic of an agent working and a human using AI is not the same. A programming agent, upon accepting a task, often has to run through 40-50 rounds between the codebase, terminal, and sandbox: reading files, calling tools, running tests, checking errors, and then modifying the code. In long-chain tasks, the cost of errors accumulates multiplicatively. A model with 99% accuracy per step has about a 60% chance of successfully completing 50 steps; a model with 95% accuracy per step has less than an 8% chance of failing after 50 steps. So companies quickly realized that when buying models, they shouldn't just look at the listed unit price on the price list, but also the total cost of getting everything done in one go. Understanding this makes the current situation of open-source models easier to comprehend. Over the past year, the token share of open-source models has increased from 11% to 19%, and the number of calls is 22.5 times that of a year ago; however, their share of expenditures has dropped from 6% to 4%. This is because most open-source models have been caught in a price war, with the average unit price falling to less than a third of its original price, now only $0.13 per million tokens, less than one-fifth of the average price of closed-source models. The open-source model did nearly one-fifth of the work but only took one-twenty-fifth of the money. Kimi's 61% success rate is precisely because it didn't fall into the $0.13 trap. On July 16th of this year, Dark Side of the Moon released the Kimi K3 with 2.8 trillion parameters. Its official API pricing is $3 for input and $15 for output, the same price as the closed-source flagship Sonnet 4.5 from a year ago, and more than three times the price of the previous generation K2.6. The K3.1 Pro, released on October 23rd, dropped to $2 and $10, still within the flagship price range. In an open-source market with an average price of $0.13, this flagship pricing strategy stems primarily from the model's performance in long contexts, native multimodal processing, and programming. But benchmark scores alone aren't enough. The weights of open-source models are public; changing a model in the inference cloud dropdown menu only requires modifying one line of configuration. Why should American companies pay more for it? This reveals one of the most troublesome engineering problems that arises when open-source models leave the lab. For data compliance and latency, most American companies don't send code and documentation directly to overseas servers; instead, they purchase hosting services from local cloud providers like Fireworks, Together, or Amazon Bedrock. However, over the past year, engineering teams in Silicon Valley have frequently discovered that a certain open-source model, which appears incredibly intelligent in official demos, inexplicably becomes unresponsive after dozens of consecutive tool calls once integrated into their production environments and using third-party inference cloud APIs. The reason lies in the fact that inference cloud is a business heavily reliant on GPU turnover. The number of requests a single GPU can handle per second directly determines a cloud provider's quarterly gross profit. To conserve GPU memory and maximize throughput, different platforms often perform different quantization and compression processes on the trillion-parameter MoE model in the background, or simplify the parsing templates for tool calls. In casual conversation, this slight reduction in precision might not be noticeable; however, within a complex agent loop of dozens of interconnected steps, the deviation is enough to cause the model to select the wrong expert, corrupt the format, and crash the entire workflow. Customers buy models based on their brand, then the project fails, and the original manufacturer ends up taking the blame. Kimi is clever; instead of issuing statements to argue with any cloud vendor, it directly open-sourced and continuously operates a vendor accuracy verification tool. Back in the K2 era, it open-sourced K2 Vendor Verifier, using the same set of tests to compare the performance of various inference clouds and official APIs in tool calls. When K2.6 was released in April of this year, this toolkit was upgraded to KVV (Kimi Vendor Verifier). The test items include regression samples of tool calls under long context, JSON schema validation, rejection of malformed calls, long memory test with millions of tokens, and 113 programming agent tasks. The results from various inference cloud providers are posted in tabular form on GitHub.

Kimi Vendor Verifier publicly compares the deployment performance of different vendors

K3.1 Pro deployment performance

Image source: Moonshot AI / GitHub

Which cloud vendor secretly reduced accuracy to save on machines? Developers can spot it at a glance on the dashboard.

To align KVV scores with the official Kimi API, Silicon Valley inference cloud vendors had to turn to Kimi engineers to fix bugs. Fireworks AI's engineering team later published a retrospective, explaining how they collaborated with the Kimi team to patch the underlying decoding barriers, clean up redundant fields in multi-turn dialogues, and ultimately refine the managed interface's tool call performance to the original manufacturer level. Most teams that do open source simply put their efforts online and leave the rest to chance. However, Dark Side of the Moon brought its rigorous quality control to the open source world: "I don't charge you admission, but I'll manage how you serve the food." This hit a nerve with enterprise procurement. For Silicon Valley tech leaders, KVV recalibrated the non-standard components scattered across various data centers into original equipment manufacturer (OEM) certified standard parts. If it were only about hosting quality, Kimi would be a useful external helper at best. Another name mentioned in the report reveals its second layer of value overseas: Cursor.

Cursor's on-site exchange with investor Accel

Image source: Accel

Menlo wrote that the proportion of AI developers doing post-training this year has increased from 6% to 10%. The most typical example is Cursor training Composer 2 on Kimi K2.5, with Fireworks providing the inference for the reinforcement learning stage. Menlo's data clearly illustrates the plight of independent application companies. Of the $176.8 billion in enterprise AI spending this year, Anthropic, OpenAI, and Google's three labs took $122.7 billion, accounting for 69%, compared to 50% a year ago. Of that, the labs' own applications accounted for $40 billion. Looking at the $34 billion programming market alone, Claude Code and Codex alone raked in $24 billion, representing 70%. The more successful the application company, the more it proves to the upstream that the market is large enough. Once the market is proven large enough, the upstream, holding the models and computing power, has more reason to get involved directly. Continuing to act only as a middleman will eventually lead to being crushed by the upstream. In early January of this year, Cursor held an internal "War Time" meeting, where founder Michael Truell demanded that everyone accelerate the development of their own models. For companies seeking to scale up, it's incredibly difficult. Cursor has the real-world interaction data of millions of programmers writing code, modifying files, and running terminal programs daily—the best fuel for reinforcement learning. However, it only has tens of thousands of GPUs, not millions, and doesn't have the time to spend half a year training a pre-training platform with trillions of parameters from scratch. Furthermore, a few days after Cursor's internal meeting, Anthropic tightened its rules, no longer allowing third-party programming tools to log in and use their personal subscription accounts. The only way forward is to borrow resources from the open-source world and focus all their efforts on the latter part of reinforcement learning. On March 19th, Cursor released Composer 2, priced at $0.50 for input and $2.50 for output, exactly one-tenth the price of Claude Opus 4.6 at the time. Cursor's Lee Robinson later stated that only about a quarter of the final model's computational power came from the base station; the rest was spent on Cursor's own training. This rewrote the standards by which application companies choose open-source models. Previously, choosing open-source models was like choosing a ready-made garment—whoever scored a few points higher on a public leaderboard was chosen. However, in the 46-page technical report appendix subsequently released by Cursor, the research team wrote that when evaluating candidate pedestals, they intentionally avoided looking at the scores of programming agent-type benchmarks, reasoning that these benchmarks have weaker predictive power for the final results because the agent's and long-term task capabilities can be significantly altered during the reinforcement learning phase. Many models, in order to look good on the day of benchmark release, are already crammed with fine-tuning for specific question banks before leaving the factory, squeezing the weight space like a water-soaked sponge; outsiders may see high scores, but if you buy them and want to add three times the reinforcement learning computing power, the model will quickly experience capability collapse. Cursor directly puts candidate models into its own testing phase. They only tested three things: the underlying coding knowledge, the ability to track the state of a file after it has been modified dozens of times, and the model's perplexity on Cursor's large private codebase. After testing, Kimi K2.5 remained. The report cited its strong overall performance and high efficiency on Cursor's own infrastructure. Through continuous pre-training and reinforcement learning, Composer 2's score on CursorBench, Cursor's own benchmark set, rose from 36.0 on the base model to 61.3, surpassing Claude Opus 4.6's 58.2. In May, Cursor launched Composer 2.5 on the same K2.5 platform. This breakthrough from spring to summer has provided a model for Silicon Valley: for top application companies, open weighted models are no longer a cost-effective alternative, but rather a starting point for the few that can adopt them and continue investing heavily in training their own assets.

Tea Money

Cursor pushes Composer 2, trained on K2.5, to its users. American companies use Kimi in their production environments, and the main providers handling this traffic are American inference clouds like Fireworks and Together.

Putting Kimi, Fireworks, and Cursor together reveals a well-defined division of labor.

A company eager to prove its commercial viability, seeing its model popular in Silicon Valley, would often immediately rent an office in San Francisco, poach a group of corporate sales staff with high salaries, and directly knock on the doors of major American clients, pocketing all the profit margin. The Dark Side of the Moon didn't do that. In July 2025, Menlo also wrote in its mid-year report that American companies' reluctance to directly call Chinese companies' APIs was one of the reasons for the stagnation of open-source model market share. This hurdle of compliance and trust cannot be crossed by sales staff flying to California and talking themselves hoarse. Instead of crashing into that wall head-on, it's better to let our American partners have the lion's share. Kimi's engineering team worked with platforms like Fireworks to fine-tune the inference engine before and after the model went live, and American companies signed contracts with American cloud providers, keeping the data in American data centers.

Microsoft's data center server racks in Quincy, Washington, USA

Image source: John Brecher / Microsoft

It is precisely because the dark side of the moon did not reach out for business that Fireworks was willing to vigorously promote Kimi, and Cursor engineers dared to build their flagship product on the K2.5 weight. Only when everyone can make money can this thing truly take off. Regarding the revenue of Dark Side of the Moon itself, it has written the rules into the K3.1 Pro license. Internal deployment, research, or fine-tuning for one's own products are all possible without prior notice. There are only two situations where negotiation is required: first, if the model is used for model hosting and inference or fine-tuning services, generating over $20 million in revenue for 12 consecutive months, a separate agreement with Dark Side of the Moon is necessary; second, if the end product has over 100 million monthly active users or over $20 million in monthly revenue, the model name must be clearly displayed on the interface. Use through official Dark Side of the Moon products or certified inference partners is not subject to these two restrictions. In August, Reuters reported that Dark Side of the Moon was in talks with Microsoft, Amazon, and Google about revenue sharing for K3-related services, asking for up to 30%. Less than a month later, on September 18th (US time), Amazon listed K3 on Bedrock. The global standard tier price was the same as Dark Side of the Moon's official price: $3 and $15, with the revenue sharing percentage not disclosed. Microsoft's approach was more circuitous. K3 entered Microsoft Foundry at the end of July, but at that time, Fireworks was running the inference in the background, and Foundry was only responsible for integration. On November 5th (US time), Microsoft announced on its blog that K3.1 Pro was officially available on Foundry. In the words of old-time business people, this is called "take the back road freely, but pay a fee for the main road." Kimi doesn't charge a penny to 99 out of 100 startups that are still experimenting; only those that actually make tens of millions of dollars a year will sit down and discuss things according to the rules. Knowing which part of the money you shouldn't earn right now sometimes requires more discipline than knowing how to make money.

Black Cat, White Cat

Browsing our focus a bit further from this 61% cross-section, the reason this set of data from this fall is so intriguing is that it presents a new relationship that has naturally grown out of the large-scale model industry after three years of adjustment.

Two years ago, the debate in Silicon Valley about the endgame of the industry was black and white: one side believed that closed-source flagships would dominate everything, and application companies would sooner or later become just a thin layer of interfaces; the other side believed that open source would turn intelligence into free tap water, making it impossible for all model companies to make money.

By 2026, neither scenario had materialized. Anthropic and OpenAI still accounted for 86% of the spending on large-scale model APIs by US companies. Wall Street investment banks reviewing cross-border M&A contracts, and pharmaceutical companies conducting zero-tolerance literature reviews, would still unhesitatingly pay for the most expensive closed-source flagships. The budget flowing to open source did not become a battleground for cheap computing power; instead, it converged on cutting-edge models like Kimi. The divide between open source and closed source was no longer a zero-sum game. Catalyzed by complex tasks, a broad boundary emerged between the two. In this intersecting area, many Silicon Valley companies that heavily utilize Kimi are also major clients of Anthropic and OpenAI. In the early stages of their products, they use the strongest closed-source models to test prototypes and validate requirements. Once a long workflow is validated, the number of calls begins to increase exponentially, or, like Cursor, they accumulate enough unique interaction data to incorporate industry experience into their weights, they turn to the open platform closest to the forefront and allowing for deep modification. In the past, model companies and application companies operated on a zero-sum game model, with one selling APIs and the other buying them. Once model companies developed their own applications, the two sides immediately became adversaries in a zero-sum game. Now, application companies are investing three-quarters of their computing power in training open models, becoming "half a model company"; the influence of model developers is no longer measured by how many tokens they sell, but also by how many other people's core products have grown from their weight.

Kimi K3.1 Pro Official Release Main Visual

Image Source: Dark Side of the Moon

The day after the Menlo report was released, on November 4th, Dark Side of the Moon released the full weights of the Kimi K3.1 Pro on Hugging Face as scheduled. According to its own published results, the Dark Side of the Month achieved a 65.7% score on Terminal-Bench 4.0, a benchmark for measuring the practical capabilities of programming agents. This is higher than GPT-6 Astra's 58.2% and only 0.7 percentage points behind Claude Opus 5.5's 66.4%. For the US team that has staked its product pipeline on an open-source platform, this 0.7 percentage point difference, along with the pace of progress every few months from K2, K2.5, K2.6 to K3, K3.1 Pro, is more reassuring than any open-source slogan. The dedicated models trained later need to be retrained every few months to keep up with the latest advancements. Choosing a platform is equivalent to choosing the company's iteration speed for the next year. In San Francisco, probably no startup would put "Our platform is from China" on the first page of their pitch presentation; the origin of the large-scale model remains a sensitive topic. But once you return to the server room where everything is running every day, back to the engineers staring at screens late into the night waiting for 50 rounds of Agent loops to complete, all slogans give way to pragmatism. Whoever catches the mouse is the good cat. When application companies across the ocean truly need a partner that can withstand the test, they can look up and see it already standing there.

data.title: Investing is a game for the few; most people are just gambling.
data.description:
As mentioned earlier, I don't write much about macroeconomics and economic crises anymore, but I still write when I feel it's particularly necessary. However, this writing is no longer about predicting the impact of a crisis on investment, but rather about explaining what I consider a very important principle in investing:

Always use spare money, and never use money that cuts into your living expenses for investment. Always keep at least 18 months' worth of living expenses, or even more, for yourself.

If you can't do this, don't participate in any investment.

But writing these kinds of articles is exhausting. If I don't get to the key points, readers might not understand or grasp the implications; if I do get to the key points, it might trigger various sensitive terms, so I often find myself in a dilemma, wasting my time.

Over the past few years, I've often encountered awkward situations when writing articles, and I've struggled with this twice for a long time.

The first time was after my second online sharing session last January, when I felt it was necessary to write some more in-depth analytical articles; the second time was when writing the "Learning from the Day" series.

In these two instances, I originally wrote longer and more articles, but after finishing them, I either repeatedly revised them for security reasons, removing sensitive words, resulting in something that was essentially useless and unnecessary to publish; or I felt I had thoroughly explored the subject, only to find it impossible to publish. Therefore, some articles, even after being written in their entirety, were ultimately deleted and not published. Furthermore, there has been an unexpected shift in my thinking over the past few years, fundamentally contradicting one of my original intentions for starting this public account. One of my key initial motivations for starting this public account was my belief that the crypto ecosystem could offer the general public a different path and opportunity than traditional investment fields, because the financial threshold for participating in the crypto ecosystem is very low, and it doesn't require the identity and regulatory barriers of traditional investment fields. Therefore, I was optimistic about public participation in the crypto ecosystem and explicitly advised the public to be bullish on Bitcoin and Ethereum. But now I completely change my perspective. Therefore, I no longer actively encourage public participation in my articles, nor do I mention participating in Bitcoin and Ethereum. I even advise the public to be cautious. Why this change? This also happened after reading Duan Yongping's investment Q&A. Duan Yongping made a very insightful statement in the Q&A (roughly): At least 85% of the general public is fundamentally unsuitable for any investment, but these 85% won't admit it. There's nothing shameful about honestly admitting you're unsuitable for any investment. Because daring to admit it is already quite remarkable, surpassing at least 85% of the public. After Duan Yongping said this, someone on Xueqiu (a Chinese investment platform) asked indignantly (roughly): If you don't participate in any investment, won't your money in the bank even keep up with inflation? Next, Duan Yongping responded with the sentence I repeatedly quoted in previous articles (the gist of which is): "Even if you can't keep up with inflation by putting your money in the bank, it's better than investing recklessly." At first glance, I thought Duan Yongping's words were very hurtful. But through my experience and observations over the past few years, I've gradually come to admit that what he said might actually be true. Moreover, I believe his statement that some people are unsuitable for any investment also includes being unsuitable for the crypto ecosystem. I can't say that at least 85% of people are unsuitable for any investment, but I think at least 50% are essentially gambling, but they think they're investing. If someone has a talent for gambling, that's fine; there are indeed people in the world who can consistently make money in casinos and become extremely wealthy. But the vast majority of people who gamble don't actually have a talent for gambling, and it's impossible for them to profit at the gambling table in the long run. I absolutely do not have that talent. In summary, after writing these articles, I can conclude that: There's a lack of new crypto projects worth writing about; I previously felt it necessary to write about macroeconomics and crisis predictions, but now I think it's unnecessary; I previously thought it was worthwhile to chase "100x coins," but now I think it's unnecessary to deliberately pursue them; if you do, great, but if not, it's better to maintain a calm investment mindset; Articles I originally wanted to write in greater depth are now unavailable due to various restrictions and sensitivities; Articles I originally wanted to write about, encouraging public participation in the crypto ecosystem, are now also unnecessary; Therefore, I have very few topics to write about now, and I'll just write about some casual observations and thoughts.

data.title: Wall Street extends an olive branch: Why did HYPE's momentum falter after its surge?
data.description:
Author: Nancy, PANews

Hyperliquid has recently become one of the hottest topics in the crypto market. From ICE extending an olive branch to legendary Wall Street investor Stanley Druckenmiller entering the fray, Hyperliquid is accelerating its move towards the stage of US institutional-grade financial infrastructure, also giving the market more imagination for this leading Perp DEX.

Driven by a series of positive news, HYPE once surged strongly, approaching its all-time high. However, the brief upward trend did not continue, and HYPE subsequently turned around and continued to decline. In addition to the overall weakening of the crypto market, the realization of previous positive news, profit-taking by large investors, market competition pressure, and concerns about selling pressure from the unlocking of team tokens were all important factors that drove its price correction.

Hyperliquid founder Jeff dons a suit as he heads to Wall Street. Recently, when Hyperliquid founder Jeff Bezos met with policymakers in Washington, D.C., he wore a dark suit and tie, conforming to the dress code of the political center. This usually low-profile crypto tycoon almost always dresses casually in T-shirts, hoodies, and shorts. Colossus previously revealed details of Jeff's minimalist lifestyle in an in-depth report, stating that he owns 15 pairs of Lululemon shorts and 10 T-shirts, usually rotating between three colors. From T-shirts and shorts to suits and ties, it's not just Jeff's style of dress that's changing; Hyperliquid, the company he founded, is also undergoing a transformation. This crypto-native platform, which once challenged Wall Street, is now gradually entering the vision of traditional finance and even beginning to gain attention and acceptance from its former rivals. At the beginning of this year, Hyperliquid broke through the trading barriers of traditional financial markets with its on-chain perpetual contract trading, challenging Wall Street's long-standing trading rules and industry moats, which also triggered dissatisfaction and resistance from traditional financial forces. However, in just a few months, the situation began to reverse. In recent months, Hyperliquid has gradually moved from being a star project in the crypto world to the broader mainstream financial stage. From Trump publicly naming it at the White House, to Stanley Druckenmiller posting his first tweet in support, Musk retweeting related news, and then to traditional financial giant ICE investing in its ecosystem project Trade.xyz. Meanwhile, in the noisy and speculative crypto market, this team of only 11 people has already established a sizable commercialization path, using real protocol revenue to support token buybacks. Hyper Screener data shows that as of November 6th, Hyperliquid's cumulative protocol revenue has exceeded $1.23 billion, of which approximately $1.2 billion was used for token buybacks, accounting for a staggering 97.5%. Recent performance also demonstrates its impressive profitability. DeFiLlama data shows that in the past 30 days, Hyperliquid's revenue reached $68.88 million, ranking third across the entire network, behind only the two major stablecoin issuers, Tether and Circle. The imagination fueled by Wall Street, coupled with continuously generated protocol revenue and large-scale token buybacks, has fueled market optimism regarding Hyperliquid, leading to a strong upward trend for HYPE. In late September of this year, HYPE reached a record high of $97.9. Although it subsequently experienced a correction, it rallied strongly again at the end of October, approaching $97, just shy of its previous high. Even without the boost of a bull market, HYPE has repeatedly challenged its historical high, becoming one of the few crypto projects capable of exhibiting independent price action. Buybacks Fails to Stop Selling Pressure: Why Has HYPE's Price Stagnated? The improved US regulatory environment, the proactive embrace from Wall Street, and strong profitability should have provided HYPE with sustained upward momentum. However, after a brief surge at the end of last month, HYPE has turned downwards and continued to decline. CoinGecko data shows that HYPE has fallen by 19.6% since its high on October 30. Aside from external shocks such as the Binance hack and the AI ​​stock sell-off triggered by the "blue tsunami" of the US midterm elections, HYPE itself has recently faced multiple pressures. As the price of HYPE approaches its historical high, some funds are choosing to take profits, especially large investors and whales who positioned themselves early on. According to Santiment data, on October 30th, four large whale wallets closed out all their long HYPE positions, netting a total profit of approximately $5 million. The largest wallet had been accumulating HYPE since late May. Lookonchain monitoring shows that on October 31st, two addresses sold a total of approximately 1.21 million HYPE, profiting over $26.5 million. Large holder Yeti0x also recently exchanged $2.49 million worth of KHYPE for HYPE and subsequently began selling it. Meanwhile, large-scale HYPE activity from multiple institutions has also raised market concerns. According to on-chain analyst Ai Yi, since October 30th, a16z has transferred a total of 233,000 HYPE tokens, worth over $20.6 million; Onchain Lens monitoring shows that FalconX transferred a total of 350,000 HYPE tokens to Coinbase within three days, worth approximately $30.57 million; on-chain analyst MLM monitoring shows that Paradigm recently unstaking 2.55 million HYPE tokens through 15 different wallets, worth approximately $224 million, but considering that Paradigm also conducted a similar large-scale unstaking operation several weeks ago, this may just be a wallet consolidation; Galaxy Digital's OTC trading department recently deposited 47,000 HYPE tokens to OKX, worth approximately $4.06 million, indicating a potential sale. Furthermore, US HYPE spot ETFs are also experiencing continuous net outflows. SoSoValue data shows that since October this year, the net outflow of HYPE spot ETFs has reached $42.14 million.

· Team Token Allocation: Market Concerns About Potential Supply Pressure

Besides short-term selling pressure from profit-taking, the allocation of team tokens is also a focus of market attention. Last month, Hyperliquid officially announced that it would unlock 180,000 HYPE tokens and planned to officially distribute them to team members on November 6, 2026. This arrangement has raised concerns in the market about potential new supply.

However, in terms of scale, the 180,000 HYPE tokens allocated this time only account for 0.075% of the current circulating supply of approximately 239 million tokens, a relatively limited proportion. In addition, the team's OTC (over-the-counter) targeted sale to specific institutions avoids direct selling pressure and price slippage from the public order book.

The uncertainties surrounding the progress of external cooperation have also weakened market expectations to some extent. Shortly after ICE announced its cooperation with Trade.xyz, planning to introduce Hyperliquid-based perpetual contracts to the US market, the institution deleted the relevant cooperation announcement, briefly sparking speculation about whether the cooperation had changed and causing temporary panic. Subsequently, ICE reissued the announcement, adjusting its wording and emphasizing that the cooperation was a "planned introduction" and "subject to regulatory approval." Therefore, whether Hyperliquid's story of opening up the US market can truly come to fruition still depends on the CFTC's approval process, and it cannot be translated into actual user growth and revenue increase in the short term. As more players enter the market with licenses, Hyperliquid faces new competition. The improvement of the US regulatory environment does not mean that Hyperliquid can exclusively enjoy the market benefits. As the regulatory framework gradually becomes clearer, more trading platforms are also accelerating their deployment. Recently, the CFTC announced the opening of perpetual futures trading for individual US stocks, with Kalshi, Coinbase Derivatives, Kraken, and Crypto.com among the first batch of companies listed. This means that Hyperliquid may face more direct competition in the US market in the future. It's worth noting that while competitors are entering the market, the Hyperliquid ecosystem is also actively seeking compliant access to the US market. HypeStrat Markets, a subsidiary of HYPE Treasury's Hyperliquid Strategies, recently revealed that it has applied to register as a CFTC Futures Commission Merchant (FCM). If approved, this FCM will be able to handle US client accounts for licensed markets deployed under the HIP-3 framework, helping the Hyperliquid ecosystem provide perpetual contract trading services to US clients within a regulated framework. Following the midterm elections, Congressional changes have created uncertainty regarding policy support. Jeff's recent trip to Washington aimed to facilitate Hyperliquid's entry into the US market, but the shifting political climate in Washington could become an uncertain factor for Hyperliquid's expansion in the US. Prior to the midterm elections, the Trump administration's friendly signals on crypto policies, the CFTC's openness to perpetual contract trading frameworks, and the cooperation plan between ICE and Trade.xyz all raised market expectations for Hyperliquid's entry into the US market. Jeff's trip to Washington at this time is also seen as a signal that the project is trying to further improve policy communication channels. However, from a timing perspective, this trip coincides with the political landscape shift following the US midterm elections. In the November 3rd midterm elections, the Democrats won control of both the House and Senate, while the Republicans lost their majority in both houses. With the change of control in Congress, the pace of progress on related crypto legislation and regulatory frameworks, as well as Congress's focus on DeFi, highly leveraged derivatives, and investor protection, may all face new uncertainties. Although Trump will continue to govern, he will face a Democratic-led Congress for the next two years, which may further constrain his legislative agenda and policy implementation. For Hyperliquid, this change could affect market assessments of its US expansion prospects. It's worth noting, however, that in a Bloomberg report, Jeff emphasized that Hyperliquid is more like the internet or Linux, focusing on providing a neutral underlying infrastructure. The report also revealed a significant detail: during the filming, the Hyperliquid team specifically requested that no portraits of current or former US presidents appear in the background of the interview. Perhaps Hyperliquid wanted to send a signal that it wasn't seeking political endorsement from a particular administration, but rather an infrastructure-like status that could function in different political environments. According to Jeff, Hyperliquid's goal from the beginning was not just to build a more efficient trading platform, but to construct a network capable of supporting the entire financial system, allowing stocks, derivatives, and even more financial activities to ultimately operate on this network. "We don't see this as building a trading platform, but as building an entire network," Jeff explained Hyperliquid's vision in a recent interview. They examined existing blockchains at the time but found none could meet the global financial market's demands for throughput and latency without significant compromises. Now, from its initial emergence as a perpetual contract trading platform to gaining attention from Wall Street institutions, and then attempting to integrate with traditional financial infrastructure, Hyperliquid is gradually expanding beyond the boundaries of the native crypto market. However, to truly move from a trading platform to financial infrastructure, entering Wall Street may only be the beginning.
