data.title: The truth behind the $3 trillion wipeout of the US stock market crash: violent deleveraging of AI.
data.description:
Overnight, US stocks lost $3 trillion.

On November 5th local time, the AI ​​industry chain was "bloodied." The Nasdaq index plummeted 5.52%, Nvidia fell 9.3%, AMD plunged 17.3%, SpaceX fell 9%, and the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index dropped 12.2%.

Even Anthropic's IPO is in jeopardy. The probability of completing its IPO before November 30th plummeted from 84% on Wednesday to 60% on Thursday afternoon. In the worst-case scenario, its valuation could be reduced from $1.8 trillion to $500 billion.

The immediate trigger was the US midterm elections, with the Democrats winning by a landslide, and the market worrying that some restrictive policies on AI might be introduced.

For example, in Texas and Georgia, candidates advocating restrictions on data center construction won the elections.

Some members of Congress even suggested suspending advanced AI development. A deeper reason is that "overheated investment and commercial returns failing to meet expectations are problems everyone is aware of," Lin Zhou (pseudonym), an entrepreneur in the field of artificial intelligence, told Pencil News. This round of AI fever may have entered a late stage. Another investor who has long followed the US technology industry told Pencil News that this is Wall Street taking the opportunity to "violently deleverage (AI). It's not a cyclical reversal of the industry's fundamentals." 01 US Data Centers, in Trouble? The first snowflake of Wall Street's avalanche fell in Texas. On November 3, Democratic candidate Gina Hinojosa defeated Republican incumbent Governor Greg Abbott, ending more than 30 years of Republican control of the governorship. This election shocked Wall Street not only because Texas is a traditional Republican stronghold, but also because it is a core market for data center construction in the United States. Texas boasts relatively cheap land, abundant energy resources, and a long-standing business-friendly policy. Tech giants like Google, Microsoft, and Meta have all established large data centers there. According to previous estimates by GLJ Research, Texas accounts for about a quarter of the data center capacity planned for operation in the United States by 2030. However, the newly elected governor is not friendly to these projects. During her campaign, Governor Inojosa promised to suspend approval of new data center projects until the state legislature passes stricter laws protecting residents' electricity and water costs and local decision-making power. She also proposed cutting data center tax breaks and requiring developers to bear their own increased grid costs. In a video released on October 22, she clearly stated that upon being elected governor, she would suspend all data center approvals until relevant protective laws are enacted. This is not an isolated incident. Georgia also welcomed a new Democratic governor. Former Atlanta Mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms won the election after promising to temporarily halt new data center construction to assess their impact on residential electricity bills, communities, and the environment. Ohio's newly elected governor, Amy Acton, also proposed a conditional construction halt policy. She requires developers to bear the costs of electrical infrastructure, meet environmental requirements, and use unionized labor in project construction. These three states all occupy important positions in the US data center industry landscape. Morgan Stanley believes that Acton's election poses a significant risk of delays to data center projects in Ohio, including a 10-gigawatt project involving Nvidia. Why are many local residents unwelcoming of data centers? Because tech companies receive massive tax breaks, while data centers require vast amounts of electricity and water. Locals worry that some of the costs of grid expansion, energy supply, and public resource consumption will ultimately be passed on to ordinary households. Research firm Redbud Consulting tracked 47 related referendums in 44 localities across 12 states in the US. Of the 45 votes that have been counted, 44 supported restricting data center construction. Goldman Sachs estimates that approximately 45% of planned new data center capacity in the US may be affected by related policies. On November 4th, AI infrastructure-related stocks were the first to be sold off. On November 5th, the decline further spread to chips, cloud computing, and large technology companies. What truly unsettles Wall Street is that the US technology industry has already invested too much money. A report released this year by the International Energy Agency shows that the capital expenditures of five large technology companies will exceed $400 billion in 2025, and are expected to grow by about 75% in 2026. They believe that AI needs more computing power, more computing power needs more chips, and more chips need larger data centers. This belief has supported the rise of global technology stocks and spawned a huge financing market. Now, are you saying that data centers can't be built in the future? 02 Is the lifeline of AI about to be strangled? After the Democrats won the election, even more surreal things followed. On November 4th, less than 24 hours after the election results were announced, Arizona Democratic Representative Yassamin Ansari publicly stated on the social media platform X: "The first priority for the Democrats on their first day in office should be to halt advanced AI research and development, regulate this out-of-control industry, and ban artificial superintelligence." Elon Musk saw this message. On November 5th, he retweeted Ansari's statement, leaving only the short sentence: "It's a Brave New World." Nikita Bier, former product manager at X and a serial entrepreneur, retweeted Ansari's post, writing in Chinese: "Thank you, Congresswoman. China supports you." More notably, Ansari's appeal was not merely verbal. As early as September 24, she and several Democratic lawmakers jointly introduced the "Ban on Artificial Superintelligence Act of 2026." This bill plans to establish a cabinet-level Artificial Intelligence Department and suspend the development of certain advanced AI systems until federal regulatory agencies establish corresponding safety rules. According to the bill's text, AI systems with training computations of 10²⁵ operations or more will be subject to the research and development suspension measures. Advanced models will also require regulatory approval before formal deployment. The bill even stipulates that individuals who intentionally or recklessly violate the relevant bans could face up to 20 years in prison. Currently, this is still a bill that has not yet passed, and it does not mean that all Democratic lawmakers have supported suspending advanced AI research and development. However, it reveals another risk facing the US AI industry. Previously, technology companies were mainly concerned about not being able to obtain enough chips, electricity, and data centers. Now, some US congressmen are beginning to raise a more fundamental question: should the development of AI models that require hundreds of billions of dollars in computing power and are constantly being trained to become more powerful continue? If the development of advanced models is strictly restricted, then data centers will face not only approval delays, but potentially a slowdown in future computing power demand growth. For companies that borrow money to buy GPUs and bet on continued growth in AI demand over the next decade, this is a policy risk that must be taken seriously. If even stronger, larger models are no longer trained, what's the point of having so many GPUs, computing power, and storage? The capital market: Forget it (just kidding). 03 Financing Environment May Deteriorate After this crash, the financing environment for AI startups will deteriorate. Anthropic originally planned to launch its IPO roadshow the week of November 9th, but potential investors are beginning to question its ability to complete the listing as planned. The most critical point of contention is valuation. Previously, Anthropic's IPO was discussed at a valuation as high as $2 trillion. Now, potential investors believe that the recently discussed $1.5 trillion valuation is still too high and are demanding a larger offering discount. Reports suggest that in the worst-case scenario, the valuation could be reduced to $500 billion. If even companies like this have to lower their valuations to successfully list, it will be difficult for smaller AI startups in the primary market with less revenue and a longer timeline for profitability to continue demanding that investors price them according to previous optimistic expectations. The tide has already receded. Firmus, the Australian data center company backed by Nvidia, withdrew its IPO. Blackstone's AirTrunk postponed its Singapore listing, and SoftBank-backed SB Energy also suspended its listing plans. Lin Zhou believes that the AI ​​industry does indeed face issues of over-investment and lower-than-expected commercial returns, and this wave of AI hype may have entered a later stage. The aforementioned investor, however, believes it's premature to say the industry boom is coming to an end. "LLM, SML, or other models represent a shift in a completely new computing paradigm, disrupting traditional programming computing models. From physical infrastructure in data centers to upper-level software applications, everything is being reconstructed by AI. The industry's 10-20 year development cycle is still in its early stages of application, but what we're currently in is a 1-3 year investment boom's clearing-out period." He said, taking AI computing power as an example, it's even scarce. "Similar to the early development stage of traditional cloud computing, AWS initially relied on Amazon's e-commerce business for revenue, but later gradually became its core revenue driver—it was a structural replacement process." Going forward, investor choices will gradually diverge. The first type of investor will continue to seek new breakthroughs in underlying technologies. "In the past few years, some AI technical challenges have not been completely solved. One approach is to continue expanding the model scale, increasing data and computing power; another approach is to find new algorithm architectures and technological paradigms," Lin Zhou believes. He thinks that some investors will focus on the latter in the future. He believes that compared to simply achieving higher scores on a particular dataset, publishing papers, or improving existing AI systems engineering, these investors will place greater emphasis on breakthroughs in underlying paradigms. They hope to find the next OpenAI or Anthropic. The second type of investor will increasingly focus on whether a company can make money. "As the AI ​​industry matures, investors will have higher requirements for a company's financial health and return on investment. Historically, after a bubble bursts, some industries will inevitably undergo a reshuffle, and some companies will die; this is normal."

data.title: Nobel laureate Argeon's lengthy article: What should governments do in the AI ​​era?
data.description:
A file photo of Philippe Arguion. Source: *Government and Market Economy Research*, 2026, No. 1

What Should Governments Do in the Age of Artificial Intelligence—A Perspective Based on the Schumpeterian Growth Paradigm

Philippe Arguion, Professor at the Collège de France, London School of Economics and Political Science, and INSEAD, 2025 Nobel Laureate in Economics.

【Abstract】Artificial intelligence is the latest form of automation technology and is being gradually applied to various fields of production and services. Based on the mechanism of the "Schumpeterian growth paradigm," this article predicts that the artificial intelligence revolution will, like the historical electricity revolution and information technology revolution, improve enterprise productivity and enhance economic growth potential.

[Abstract] Artificial intelligence is the latest form of automation technology and is being gradually applied to various fields of production and services. Based on the mechanism of the "Schumpeterian growth paradigm," this article predicts that the artificial intelligence revolution will, like the historical electricity revolution and information technology revolution, improve enterprise productivity and enhance economic growth potential.

This technological revolution may also bring about a Schumpeterian growth dilemma, exacerbate income inequality, and have a significant impact on the economic development and social environment of countries around the world. Therefore, governments need to adopt a series of policies to address these impacts, including implementing industrial policies that encourage innovation and competition, improving education systems, perfecting social security systems, adjusting income redistribution, and engaging in multi-dimensional international cooperation. [Keywords] Artificial Intelligence; Schumpeterian Growth Paradigm; Industrial Policy; New Government Functions I. Introduction Since Turing proposed the "Imitation Game" (Turing Test) in 1950, research on Artificial Intelligence (AI) has a history of over 70 years. In 2012, AlexNet ignited the deep learning revolution. Modern generative AI, centered on large-scale pre-trained models, represents a completely new technological paradigm and has been gradually introduced into various fields of production and services. Joseph Schumpeter proposed the concept of "creative destruction" to describe the process by which innovation replaces old technologies, making them obsolete. The rise and development of AI technology over the past decade is the latest manifestation of this concept. Based on the "Schumpeterian growth paradigm" constructed and expanded by Aghion and Howitt (1992) and other related literature, this paper predicts that the AI ​​revolution will have a huge impact on the economic development of countries around the world. First, the innovation and application of AI will affect the economic growth potential of various countries. On the one hand, AI incentivizes innovation activities and investment, promotes innovation in leading companies, and increases the rate of new entrants. As the technology matures and spreads, AI will bring significant productivity improvements. On the other hand, AI inhibits innovation activities in non-cutting-edge enterprises. Those lagging behind in technological advancements are often impacted by intense competition, leading to an increase in their exits and a reduction in jobs. Capital, employment, data, and other resources are redistributed among industries, enterprises, and nations. Secondly, the development and application of AI may also trigger a Schumpeterian growth dilemma. The Schumpeterian growth paradigm posits that technological innovation is endogenous, stemming from entrepreneurial activity driven by the prospect of innovation rents. Data, computing power, and algorithms are all production factors required for AI technological innovation. The existence of innovation rents encourages AI technology companies to invest heavily in these production factors, making it easy for them to build extremely high competitive barriers, leading to monopolies and hindering new entrants and further innovation. Finally, AI development will have a structural impact on income distribution. The development of AI requires significant investment in computing power, data, and algorithms, exhibiting a marked "capital bias" that leads to a decline in the share of labor income. The direct impact of AI on employment is primarily reflected in the interplay between "substitution" and "complementarity." Traditional automation technologies mainly replace repetitive manual labor (such as assembly line work), but AI, especially large-scale models, has begun to replace repetitive mental labor. Highly skilled workers, such as top scientists or designers, can leverage AI to increase output tenfold or even a hundredfold, earning a higher share of income and widening the gap with ordinary workers. How should the government respond to the significant economic impact of AI technology? First, the government should actively implement industrial policies that promote innovation and competition, avoid over-regulation, tolerate innovation rents, prevent monopoly rents, and simultaneously increase investment in AI technology infrastructure, lower barriers to entry for enterprises, protect innovation and competition, and alleviate the Schumpeterian growth dilemma caused by AI technology. Second, governments should improve the education system, focusing on "learning how to learn," cultivating strong computational and reading skills, and strengthening basic education so that both minors and adults can better adapt to the social changes brought about by AI technology. Third, governments should use tax policies to regulate income distribution, expand the functions of government agencies, improve the labor market, and establish a system combining unemployment relief and training programs to build a sound social model needed for this AI revolution. Fourth, governments should commit to international cooperation, including consultation and cooperation on AI technology production infrastructure, data privacy, algorithmic bias, and intellectual property rights. The second part of this paper introduces the development path of AI technology and the Schumpeterian growth paradigm. The third part analyzes how AI technology affects economic growth. The fourth part discusses what policies and measures governments can take to address the economic impact of AI technology. The fifth part is the conclusion. II. AI and the Schumpeterian Growth Paradigm (I) A Brief History of AI Development The history of AI development can be traced back to the Turing Test, which laid the philosophical foundation for AI technology. At the Dartmouth Conference in 1956, John McCarthy first formally proposed the term "artificial intelligence." At that time, AI developed in the form of deductive rules of the "if...then..." type, a symbolic approach based on reasoning and instructions. From 1956 to the 1990s, the symbolic approach dominated, but it faced a bottleneck in knowledge acquisition, struggled to exhaust all rules, lacked learning ability, and had extremely poor generalization. In the late 1980s and 1990s, the machine learning revolution gave rise to a new approach to AI: statistical learning theory. Statistical methods gradually replaced symbolic methods, but symbolic methods were not completely abandoned. Unlike symbolic methods, statistical methods do not involve explicit human instructions. Instead, they learn to recognize associations using a set of training data and then apply these associations to new data to perform tasks. With advancements in machine learning, increased availability of data, and enhanced computing power, statistical methods have continuously evolved and improved. In 2006, Hinton proposed Deep Belief Networks, solving the optimization challenges of deep networks through layer-by-layer pre-training, marking a significant milestone in the rapid development of "deep learning." In 2012, AlexNet won the ImageNet image recognition competition with a huge advantage, its deep convolutional network structure demonstrating unprecedented learning capabilities. Subsequently, the deep learning boom ignited AI technological innovation, a true general-purpose technological revolution. In 2018, OpenAI released the Generative Pre-trained Transformer (GPT), marking the beginning of the era of large-scale AI models. The emergence of generative AI models, especially large-scale products like ChatGPT and DeepSeek, represents an unprecedented acceleration in the AI ​​revolution. For example, it took Netflix two and a half years to reach one million subscribers, and Instagram two and a half months, while ChatGPT reached that number in just five days. The continuous iteration of generative AI technology is gradually and deeply integrating into human life. The development of various industries, including the economy, public services, work organization, culture, and media, will all be inseparable from and influenced by the application and innovation of AI. (II) The Schumpeterian Growth Paradigm Aghion and Howitt (1992) constructed an endogenous growth model based on Schumpeter's innovation theory, proposing a new growth paradigm, the "Schumpeterian growth paradigm." Aghion and Howitt (1996) further expanded this growth paradigm by distinguishing between research and development to characterize the innovation activities of different firms. Aghion et al. (2025) introduced the concept of resetting the innovation clock to describe the ways and channels through which technological progress promotes economic growth. This concept argues that the increasing difficulty of improving existing technologies eventually leads to existing firms exhausting their creativity and exiting the market. However, their exit paves the way for new entrants, who generate new technologies through R&D, thus "resetting the innovation clock." This innovation reset process generates sustained long-term endogenous economic growth. This paper further enriches Schumpeter's growth theory. The Schumpeterian growth paradigm is based on three main ideas. The first is the endogenous drive of innovation. Long-term growth is driven by the cumulative process of innovation, with each innovator building upon the work of their predecessors. Innovation is not an exogenous random event, but a rational choice made by economic agents based on a trade-off between expected benefits and costs. The second is that innovation stems from entrepreneurial activity driven by the prospect of innovation rents. When firms or individuals innovate, they develop a new product or find a cheaper way of production, and before being superseded by subsequent innovations, they earn monopoly rents for a period of time. The third is "creative destruction," where innovation replaces old technologies. Interestingly, this paradigm contains a paradox: the Schumpeterian growth dilemma. On the one hand, the existence of innovation rents helps incentivize innovation and investment. On the other hand, yesterday's innovators tend to use their rents to deter subsequent entrants and innovations because they don't want to be affected by "creative destruction." Resolving this contradiction is crucial for market economy regulation and government policy implementation. The Schumpeterian growth paradigm has two main corollaries. The first is a positive correlation between economic growth and creative destruction. There are three types of measures of creative destruction: the rate of new firm entry, firm turnover (the ratio of firm entry to exit), and job turnover (the ratio of job creation to job loss). Aghion (2024) analyzed data from EU countries and found a positive correlation between measures of creative destruction and GDP growth per capita in different regions or countries. This is a unique prediction of Schumpeterian growth theory: economies need new firms to drive growth. The second corollary is that more intense competition promotes innovation by firms at the technological forefront but inhibits innovation by firms at the non-leading edge. Competition motivates leading firms to work harder and innovate more to maintain their leading position. Firms lagging behind in technology are often impacted by intense competition, leading to reduced innovation. The more developed a country is, the more cutting-edge enterprises it has compared to non-cutting-edge enterprises, the more intense the product market competition, and the greater its contribution to economic growth. (III) Introducing AI into the Schumpeterian Growth Paradigm The Schumpeterian growth paradigm emphasizes that innovation is the core of economic growth, while creative destruction is the result of innovation. Merriam-Webster's Collegiate Dictionary defines AI as "the ability of machines to mimic human intelligent behavior." Legg and Hutter (2007) argue that AI is the ability of intelligent agents to achieve goals in a wide range of environments. Aghion et al. (2019) believe that AI is the latest form of automation technology, enabling the automation of tasks that were previously impossible to automate. Aghion et al. (2019) introduced AI as a capital good capable of automating both the production of goods and the production of new ideas into the analytical framework of endogenous growth theory. This is an important attempt to incorporate AI into the Schumpeterian growth paradigm. Their research found that in task-oriented production functions, AI is a special type of capital that can substitute for conventional labor and capital in production. If production tasks are substitutable, AI technology represents “capital-embodied, skill-biased technical change”; if tasks are complementary, AI technology represents “labor-embodied, skill-biased technical change”, which differs significantly from traditional capital. In particular, they proposed that AI can promote the production of ideas, which is more effective in driving technological progress and productivity growth than simply automating the production of goods and services, thereby promoting economic growth. AI improves production efficiency by optimizing production processes and eliminating outdated technologies, while simultaneously promoting intellectual output, enhancing innovation capabilities, fostering new industries, and driving technology diffusion. With its powerful innovation capabilities, widespread "creative destruction" effect, and high technology diffusion, AI technology, as the most disruptive form of innovation today, aligns with the key mechanisms of the Schumpeterian growth paradigm. III. Is the AI ​​Revolution Beneficial to Economic Growth? (I) Microeconomic Evidence of the AI ​​Revolution Promoting Economic Growth How can data confirm that the AI ​​revolution can promote economic growth? Czarnitzki et al. (2023) used unique survey data on the adoption of AI technology by German companies, including their cross-sectional and panel datasets, to estimate the impact of AI on firm productivity. They found a significant positive correlation between AI use and enterprise productivity. This result is very robust and holds true across different measures of AI use, such as indicators of AI adoption and the intensity with which enterprises use AI methods in their business processes. Brynjolfsson et al. (2025) studied the impact of the introduction of generative AI on employee productivity after a Fortune 500 company in the United States granted its employees ChatGPT access. This company specializes in business process software, and its customer service representatives primarily provide software technical support to small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) in the United States. Suppose that a manager of an SME calls the company saying, "I want to install software, but I don't know how." The customer is then transferred to employees, some of whom are actually located in the Philippines, who guide the customer through the software installation process and manage the entire installation process. These employees are gradually granted ChatGPT access. This study used the difference-in-differences method to compare the productivity differences between employees who had ChatGPT access and other employees with similar characteristics who had not yet obtained ChatGPT access. It found that access to ChatGPT led to a significant increase in productivity. Measured by indicators such as the number of problems solved per hour, productivity increased by 14% one month after the introduction of ChatGPT and further increased to 25% two months later. (II) The Macroeconomic Effects of the AI ​​Revolution on Economic Growth and Its Estimation The above microeconomic data analysis shows that the introduction of AI significantly improved enterprise productivity. How can we analyze the role of AI in promoting economic growth from a macroeconomic perspective? Aghion et al. (2019) focused on the theoretical mechanism analysis of AI's promotion of economic growth, arguing that the impact of AI on economic growth has both temporary and permanent characteristics. As a general-purpose technology, AI can promote enterprise productivity during the diffusion period; once diffusion is complete, the growth effect will gradually fade, which is the short-term effect of AI on economic growth. If AI can continuously create new tasks, new industries, and new demands, then it will become part of the "innovation production function" of the endogenous growth model. For example, AI can facilitate the generation of new ideas by recombining existing ideas and improving the selection process within the set of possibilities, thereby permanently increasing the long-term economic growth rate. How to estimate the macroeconomic effects of the AI ​​revolution on economic growth? The first approach is to infer from the impact of past technological revolutions on economic growth. For example, electrical technology or information technology (IT) were revolutionary within a decade or longer of widespread application. These technologies improved productivity by restructuring the combination of production factors and optimizing the efficiency of economic activities, becoming the core engine driving economic growth. If the breakthroughs of the AI ​​revolution are on the same scale as the electrical and information technology revolutions, then a similar increase in overall productivity can be expected. The second approach is to use a task-based method for estimation. Because we know that AI can automate the production tasks of goods and services, we can start from this point and predict what the results will be when AI automates certain tasks.

1. Inferring from the History of Technological Revolutions

We take the driving force of the US electricity and internal combustion engine revolution in the 1920s and the information technology revolution after World War II on economic growth as examples to infer the impact of AI on economic growth. The book "The Rise and Fall of American Growth" argues that 1870 marked the beginning of high-speed growth in the modern world, with the peak growth period being half a century from 1920 to 1970; the high-speed growth brought about by electronic computers and information technology, which began to take shape in the 1970s, was mainly concentrated between 1994 and 2004. Data from the book on the average annual growth rate of total factor productivity (TFP) per decade from 1900 to 2014 shows that the average annual growth rate of US TFP was 13% from 1930 to 1939.

... Assuming that total factor productivity (TFP) or average annual economic growth rate was 1% before the electricity revolution, it reached 23% between 1930 and 1939, before returning to 1%. Similarly, the information technology revolution emerged in the United States after World War II. Personal computers became widespread in the US in the 1980s, and the 1990s saw a surge in computer and internet revolutions. The increase in US TFP in the 1990s was primarily driven by the widespread application of information technology. According to the French Commission on Artificial Intelligence (Commission del'Intelligence Artificielle, 2024), the GDP growth curve will be steeper in the decade following the AI ​​revolution because growth will be boosted during that period, after which the curve will return to its original state, parallel to the curve without AI. If the AI ​​revolution is on the same order of magnitude as the breakthroughs in the electricity and information technology revolutions, then the potential additional GDP growth rate could be expected to be between 0.8% and 13%. 2. Using a Task-Based Approach to Estimate the Impact of AI on Economic Growth. From a macroeconomic perspective, a task-based approach can also be used to analyze the positive impact of AI on economic growth. Acemoglu (2025) expanded upon the task-based model proposed by Acemoglu and Restrepo (2018, 2019) to estimate the impact of AI on total factor productivity (TFP). He found that the increase in TFP brought about by AI was relatively small, with an average annual growth of no more than 0.064%, which is one-tenth of the average annual increase in TFP brought about by the information technology revolution. Acemoglu (2025) argued that the TFP gains over a decade were the product of the following four factors: (1) the share of GDP exposed to AI tasks; (2) the share of these exposed tasks that AI introduced to generate profits; (3) the labor share adjusted for AI exposure; and (4) the labor cost savings brought about by AI. Acemoglu (2025) found these four data points based on existing literature, ultimately concluding that AI brings an average annual productivity increase of 0.064%. However, if we re-examine these data, we can find some shortcomings in Acemoglu's (2025) calculations. First, regarding the share of tasks exposed to AI in GDP, Acemoglu (2025) adopted the conclusion of Eloundou et al. (2024)—19.9%. We believe this figure is too low; Pizzinelli et al. (2023) gave a more optimistic estimate of the share of tasks exposed to AI, suggesting a range from 18% to 68%, while Acemoglu (2025) essentially took the lower limit of this range. Second, for those tasks exposed to AI, we need to identify which tasks actually benefit from introducing AI. Acemoglu (2025) used the estimate from Svanberg et al. (2024)—based on the current cost of installing and using AI systems—that 23% of vision tasks exposed to AI could become profitable through AI automation. However, the paper argues that costs will decrease over time, increasing the share of tasks profitable through AI, or defined as "the share of tasks where AI can be used for profit." Svanberg et al. (2024) simulated three scenarios where the cost of installing and using AI systems decreased by 10%, 20%, and 50%, respectively. Correspondingly, 10 years later, 30%, 50%, and 80% of vision tasks exposed to AI could be automated and profitable, respectively. Therefore, a reasonable value for the share of tasks where AI can be used for profit should not be just 23%, but rather 23%–80%. Even so, our estimate may still be somewhat conservative, as computer vision tasks are not the fastest-growing area for AI adoption. For example, in areas like comprehension, writing, or language, AI adoption is much faster than in vision. This underestimation bias caused by focusing solely on visual tasks has not yet been taken into account. Finally, regarding the labor cost savings brought about by AI, Acemoglu (2025) selected 27%, which is the average of 40% found by Noy and Zhang (2023) and 14% labor cost savings brought about by AI short-term application after one month in the study by Brynjolfsson et al. (2025). However, the latter also found that labor cost savings would increase to 25% after using AI for two to three months. If we use the 25% figure, then the labor cost savings brought about by AI should be between 33% and 40%. Based on the above three points of analysis, the report "AI: France's Ambition" (Commission del'Intelligence Artificielle, 2024) estimates that within a decade of large-scale AI application, the annual impact of AI on total factor productivity will be approximately 0.08% to 1.24%, which is much more optimistic than Acemoglu's (2025) estimate. It is worth noting that the above estimates do not yet take into account the fact that AI can not only automate tasks in the production of goods and services, but also endogenously promote the production of ideas. Furthermore, the report provides a relatively comprehensive predictive analysis of the impact of AI on the macroeconomy. If AI only automates tasks in the production of goods and services, we will see that the potential GDP curve with AI will be steeper during the ten years of AI use, and after ten years, the potential GDP curve will be parallel to the potential GDP curve without AI. However, the reality is not so simple, because AI also improves innovation technology—improves the technology of producing ideas—and we get another potential GDP growth curve, which has a higher growth rate in the first decade because it includes both the short-term and long-term effects of AI on productivity improvement; even after ten years, it can maintain higher growth even without AI, because AI has permanently improved innovation technology, that is, improved the technology that drives productivity growth, making the long-term potential economic growth rate higher. IV. New Government Functions Adapting to the Development of AI Technology (I) Industrial Policies to Promote Innovation and Competition in Response to the Schumpeterian Growth Dilemma As mentioned above, the Schumpeterian growth paradigm contains the Schumpeterian growth dilemma, namely, the existence of innovation rents helps to incentivize innovation activities and innovation investment; however, existing innovators tend to use their rents to prevent subsequent entry and innovation, leading to increased monopolies and decreased competition. Aghion et al. (2019) pointed out that the AI ​​era requires a redesign of institutions. Whether AI can promote inclusive growth depends on whether institutions can guide technological change towards "enhancing humanity" rather than simply "replacing humanity." If AI primarily replaces existing tasks, growth may stagnate; if AI continues to create new tasks that humans could not previously accomplish (such as complex data analysis and personalized education), then innovation-driven growth is sustainable. Historical data confirms the existence of the Schumpeterian growth dilemma. Robert Gordon (2018) pointed out that the growth rate of total factor productivity in the United States rose sharply between 1995 and 2005, but then declined sharply. The main reason for the change in productivity was the rise and maturation of the information technology revolution. Initially, the information technology revolution drove productivity growth. But as the information technology revolution progressed, superstar companies emerged—Google, Walmart, and Microsoft. These companies initially utilized the growth potential brought by the information technology revolution, growing stronger through mergers and acquisitions and becoming ubiquitous. These pioneering innovators, leveraging IT to drive US growth, have become increasingly large, wielding pricing power and increasing market concentration. This ultimately hinders the entry of new innovative companies, largely explaining the decline in US growth. De Loecker et al. (2020) confirmed this Schumpeterian growth dilemma using micro-data from US firms. They systematically calculated the average markup (or price-cost margin) of US firms between 1950 and 2014, finding that the markup rose from approximately 18% in 1980 to approximately 67% in 2014, while the dispersion of the markup distribution also increased significantly (greater differences in markup rates among different firms), indicating a worsening "winner-takes-all" phenomenon. This upward trend is prevalent across multiple industries, particularly prominent in manufacturing, services, and information technology. This study reveals that rising market power or monopoly leads to a systemic decline in market competition and may inhibit innovation and long-term growth. Subsequent studies have also found similar trends in rising markups in economies such as Europe and Japan. Now, the emergence and development of AI technology may, like the previous information technology revolution, repeat the Schumpeterian growth dilemma. For example, the upstream segments of the AI ​​value chain, especially in cloud computing, are dominated by a few superstar companies. Amazon, Google, and Microsoft dominate the cloud computing market, and NVIDIA is the absolute leader in the global graphics processing unit (GPU) market. AI has enormous growth potential, but the lack of competition in the upstream segments of the AI ​​value chain makes it easy for these large companies to build industry barriers, hindering future innovation and development in the AI ​​industry. We recommend that governments adopt industrial policies that promote innovation and competition, avoiding over-regulation, tolerating a certain degree of innovation rent for companies, and ensuring that companies do not use their rent to prevent new entrants. First, governments should promote open source and simplify data acquisition processes. Crucially, excessive regulation should be avoided, as large companies know how to navigate regulation, while smaller new entrants do not. We also advocate extending the European Digital Markets Act—regulations governing data management and access—to the entire AI value chain to ensure competition. Otherwise, we risk facing the negative impacts of the information technology revolution again. Second, governments should tolerate a certain level of innovation rents, allowing businesses to grow. We know that vibrant economies are those with numerous active startups that are allowed to grow. Punishing companies once they grow large, slowing them down, harms their incentive to innovate. Governments should guarantee entry, growth, and the ability for companies to earn rents through innovation, thus incentivizing them to innovate; but simultaneously, they must ensure that these rents are not used to stifle or disrupt innovation. This is key to government-driven industrial policies promoting innovation and competition, and is central to ensuring AI promotes economic growth. Third, we recommend that governments increase investment in infrastructure for production factors such as computing power and data storage, reduce barriers to entry for new enterprises, and protect innovation. Governments should orderly open up public data (such as medical data and transportation data) to provide data support for AI research and development. For example, the EU's Data Governance Act allows public data to be used for AI research and development. (II) Improve the education system, with education investment focusing on "learning how to learn." The rapid development of artificial intelligence technology has varying impacts on different jobs across industries. Gmyrek et al. (2023) decomposed work into tasks and examined the possibility that different tasks constituting a job position could be replaced by generative AI. They assigned lower scores to tasks with low substitution risk, medium scores to tasks with medium substitution risk, and higher scores to tasks with high substitution risk. They found that most management-related tasks fell into the low substitution risk category, while clerical support roles, such as typists, word processors, travel consultants, and clerks, were more likely to be replaced by AI. The impact of AI on employment is not simply "replacement," but rather "restructuring," leading to a surge in demand for highly skilled positions requiring critical thinking, creativity, and complex problem-solving abilities. The traditional education system, centered on "knowledge transmission," neglects the cultivation of "how to learn," making it difficult for students to adapt to the demands of a rapidly evolving technological society. In the AI ​​era, lifelong learning becomes essential for survival. Therefore, the government urgently needs to systematically reform the education system. The core of this reform is shifting from "teaching knowledge" to "teaching skills," enabling students to master core methods of "how to learn," cultivating strong computational and reading abilities, strengthening basic education, and reconstructing educational philosophies and curriculum systems. The essence of "learning how to learn" is to cultivate metacognitive abilities, meaning students can proactively plan learning goals, monitor the learning process, evaluate learning outcomes, and use AI to assist learning in solving practical problems. Computational ability in the AI ​​era is not simply mathematical calculation, but rather logical thinking, algorithmic thinking, and data analysis skills. These abilities are the foundation for understanding and applying AI, and are also core competencies for future jobs. Simultaneously, the information explosion in the AI ​​era requires individuals to quickly filter effective information, distinguish truth from falsehood, and possess cross-text analysis and deep reading abilities. Overall, educational reform is not merely a passive adjustment to cope with technological shocks, but a strategic measure to proactively shape the future labor market and promote social equity and inclusive growth, enabling both minors and adults to better adapt to the social changes brought about by AI technology. (III) Improving Tax Policies for Income Redistribution, Expanding New Functions of Government Agencies, and Establishing an "AI Social Adaptation Committee" As a general-purpose technology, AI is ubiquitous and will be introduced into many fields, including production, education, healthcare, finance, and other application scenarios. AI's "creative destruction" will exacerbate the income gap between capital and labor, widen the wage gap between high-skilled and low-skilled workers, and give rise to a new form of monopolistic profits by "superstar companies," posing a serious challenge to existing social models. The government can use tax policies to regulate income distribution, expand new functions of government agencies, improve the labor market, form a system combining unemployment relief and training programs, and build a social model adapted to AI technology to ensure the widespread sharing and sustainable development of technological dividends. First, tax policy is an important tool for regulating income redistribution. Governments can use progressive taxes, capital gains taxes, and special taxes for AI companies to convert the wealth generated by the AI ​​revolution into funds for redistribution. For example, Sweden and Germany have begun discussing a "robot tax," aiming to regulate the employment impact of automation through taxation and allocate funds for unemployment relief and training. Second, social problems in the AI ​​era not only involve the economic field but also multiple areas such as health, psychology, and social integration. Governments need to adjust their institutional setup and expand the functions of public health and social security departments to address these new challenges. Public health management departments could establish a branch, the "Public Health and Digital Health Department," to handle health issues brought about by AI. For example, it could focus on health inequalities caused by the digital divide, address mental health issues brought about by AI (such as anxiety and depression due to unemployment), and provide mental health services. Furthermore, the social security department should be reorganized into a "Department of Social Security and Employment Support" to address the frictional costs of occupational transitions and integrate functions related to unemployment relief, skills training, and employment services, forming a three-pronged system of "unemployment relief + skills training + employment services." This system could be funded through a combination of government tax revenue, private insurance, and individual training accounts, granting workers the right to choose training programs, promoting diversified market supply, and thus improving the labor market. Third, the government could also establish an "AI Social Adaptation Committee," composed of representatives from finance, education, health, and social security departments, to coordinate policies across departments, ensure policy consistency, and regularly assess the social impact of AI and adjust policies accordingly. The government's construction of a social model adapted to AI needs to balance inclusivity and adaptability, ensuring that different groups can participate in the AI ​​revolution, thereby guaranteeing the fair use of AI technology and avoiding discrimination and prejudice. (iv) Promoting and Regulating AI Technology Development Through International Cooperation The development and application of AI technology has transcended national borders and generated global impact. From the transnational deployment of computing infrastructure to the cross-border flow of data, from the cross-domain influence of algorithmic decisions to the ownership of intellectual property rights for AI-generated content, the governance challenges brought by AI have a distinct "global" characteristic. That is, policies of a single country are insufficient to address them, and a new global governance system adapted to the AI ​​era must be built through international cooperation. This new dimension of cooperation covers multiple key areas such as infrastructure construction related to core AI production factors, data privacy, algorithmic bias, and intellectual property rights. It requires all countries to reach consensus rules through multilateral consultation based on respect for sovereignty. First, cooperation on AI technology-related infrastructure is the physical cornerstone of global governance. The development of AI is highly dependent on infrastructure, including computing power (such as GPUs), 5G/6G networks, and data centers. These facilities are unevenly distributed globally and have strong externalities. Currently, global computing resources are highly concentrated in the United States and China, while developing countries in Africa and Latin America face computing power shortages. This uneven distribution may lead to "computing power monopolies," hindering global AI innovation. Therefore, the international community urgently needs to coordinate to avoid monopolies and promote the fair allocation of computing resources and technology transfer. Simultaneously, greening infrastructure is key to the sustainable development of AI. The high energy consumption of data centers and the carbon emissions from AI training need to be addressed through international emissions reduction cooperation. In 2023, the United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP28) included "AI computing power emissions reduction" on its agenda for the first time, calling on countries to develop carbon footprint standards for AI computing power and promote the construction of green data centers. Only through global coordination can trade barriers such as "carbon tariffs" be avoided and fair competition in the AI ​​industry be promoted. Secondly, data privacy protection is one of the most pressing issues in global AI governance. AI relies on massive amounts of data to operate, and the cross-border flow of data is a prerequisite for AI globalization. However, the laws related to data privacy protection vary greatly among different countries. For example, the EU's General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) emphasizes "data sovereignty." This fragmentation of rules leads to a surge in compliance costs for multinational corporations and hinders the global application of AI technology (such as the cross-border sharing of medical AI data). We urgently need a set of harmonized and unified international data privacy rules to balance the cross-border flow of data with sovereignty protection. In 2023, the G20's Guidelines on Free Flow of Data and Privacy Protection, the World Trade Organization (WTO) e-commerce negotiation outcomes, the APEC Cross-Border Privacy Rules Framework (CBPR), and the data provisions in the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership (RCEP) all provide new ideas for global data governance and can serve as the cornerstone for building a global data governance architecture. Third, algorithmic bias and AI ethics are value dimensions of global governance. AI systems are profoundly impacting key social areas such as judicial decisions, credit approvals, and recruitment screenings, but their inherent biases and discrimination risks may cause systemic harm to vulnerable groups. More worryingly, the misuse of deepfake and AI surveillance technologies is eroding the foundations of security and peaceful development. The UNESCO 2021 Recommendation on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence is an important milestone, but it lacks binding force. The international community urgently needs to establish a "Global Convention on AI Ethics." Fourth, the reshaping of intellectual property rules is the economic dimension of global AI governance. The traditional intellectual property system is based on the assumption of "human creators," while the copyright of AI-generated content, the boundaries of fair use of AI training data, and the patent ownership of AI-assisted inventions all raise profound new legal issues. Differences in relevant rules among countries may escalate into a technological cold war and an intellectual property trade war. The World Intellectual Property Organization (WIPO) has initiated a dialogue process between AI and intellectual property, and has begun accepting AI patent applications. However, it needs to further clarify the criteria for determining the "inventiveness of AI inventions" to achieve mutual recognition of AI patents globally. The United Nations held a high-level meeting of the "Global Dialogue on Artificial Intelligence Governance" mechanism on September 25, 2025, providing a platform for countries to build global rules adapted to the development of AI technology through multilateral consultation. The ultimate goal of global AI governance is to ensure that this transformative technology serves the common good of humanity, avoids "technological hegemony" and the "digital divide," and reduces inequality between countries. V. Conclusion Every update and application of AI in production, services, and thought production reshapes the old industrial landscape and drives the redistribution of resources. This process highly aligns with the "creative destruction" described in the Schumpeterian growth paradigm. All industries will be impacted by the AI ​​revolution. AI can both stimulate economic growth and potentially trigger a Schumpeterian growth dilemma, exacerbating income and educational inequalities and disrupting the existing social environment. Therefore, governments should adopt systematic policy measures to address these impacts. Implementing industrial policies that encourage innovation and competition is crucial for ensuring economic growth. This involves allowing businesses to enter and grow, earning innovation rents, while ensuring that the growth of established businesses does not come at the expense of new entrants. Governments should also improve education systems, utilize tax policies to regulate income distribution, expand the functions of government agencies, and build social governance models adapted to the development of AI technology. Furthermore, the balanced development of AI technology requires multilateral consultation and cooperation among governments across multiple dimensions, including AI-related infrastructure, data privacy, algorithmic bias, and intellectual property rights.
